title: Nature and States of Matter
scope_note: Earlier foundation requires source reconciliation; quantitative latent heat is SCOPE_REVIEW
introduction: Matter is not continuous like coloured paint; its particle-scale motion and interactions explain a remarkable range of visible phenomena. This unit builds a connected description from particles to states, diffusion, changes of phase and energy transfer, always separating observation from model and checking what stays conserved.

subtopics.title: Particle nature of matter
subtopics.entry_question: A drop of dye spreads through still water. What unseen moving entities can explain this change?
core1a_paragraphs: Pure substances and mixtures are made of small particles: atoms, molecules or ions, depending on the substance. These particles are not tiny coloured droplets; they are entities whose motion and interactions produce the large-scale behaviour we can observe.

A sample of water looks continuous to the eye, but adding a trace of dye allows us to infer particle motion through gradual spreading. An inference is different from a direct photograph: dye diffusion supports the particle model, but one observation alone does not reveal the precise size of a molecule.

Particle models must distinguish what is conserved from what changes. When water evaporates, individual water molecules leave the liquid. Their identity remains H₂O in an ordinary phase change. The overall number of molecules is conserved only in a closed system.
subtopics.representation: Draw a beaker before and after mixing using distinguishable particle dots. Keep the same particle count in the closed-beaker diagram; vary positions rather than transforming water molecules into new species.

worked_example.problem: Dye distributes through a closed glass of water without stirring. Does matter need to be created for the colour to become uniform?
steps: Identify the closed system and its initial dye particles.
Allow dye and water particles to move and redistribute.
The dye occupies more positions, not more total particles.
Conservation and motion together explain uniform colour.
worked_example.result: No dye is created; mixing redistributes particles.
worked_example.check: A particle ledger remains constant for the closed system.

misconception.wrong: The coloured substance multiplies as it spreads.
misconception.why: Spreading is redistribution rather than production of new dye.
misconception.repair: Track a fixed set of dye particles through successive snapshots.

demands.title: Particle mechanism for spreading
demands.core1a_explanation: Link invisible random molecular motion to visible changes in concentration; distinguish observation from inference.
demands.worked_reasoning: A clear region becomes slightly coloured as dye particles cross into it and redistribute while total particle number stays fixed.
demands.independent_check: Check conservation for a declared system boundary.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: Explain why a tiny coloured drop can eventually tint the entire closed beaker without adding more dye.
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: Colour spreading creates extra particles
core1b.repair: Draw a fixed-count particle picture and track redistribution.
core1b.boundary: What changes when the container is open and some solvent evaporates?
core1b.model_response: Dye particles move through the water and spread from the concentrated region until their distribution is roughly uniform. Closed-system particle count stays fixed.

demands.title: Choose a particle model over a reaction model
demands.core1a_explanation: An observation of uniform colour does not establish formation of a new chemical substance. A model must predict a distinguishing observation.
demands.worked_reasoning: Simple diffusion changes position and concentration; reaction changes species identities. A colour change could have either cause in other experiments.
demands.independent_check: A model prediction must be distinguishable from a compatible alternative.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: A red solute disperses without gas, heat or precipitate. What simple model best explains the uniform red appearance, and what would further test it?
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: Any change of colour must indicate a chemical reaction
core1b.repair: Test whether the species identity actually changes, not merely its location.
core1b.boundary: Would a colourless product of a chemical reaction invalidate colour as the sole diagnostic?
core1b.model_response: Mixing/diffusion is a defensible initial model. A test could compare dissolved solute identity before and after, or reverse the concentration by evaporation/recrystallisation where suitable.

demands.title: What can the observation establish?
demands.core1a_explanation: A photograph of a uniform solution does not prove the detailed mechanism or precise molecular size. Scientific arguments distinguish inference from directly observed facts.
demands.worked_reasoning: Uniform colour is compatible with many particle motions; it cannot uniquely reveal the particle's mass or bond structure.
demands.independent_check: Reject deductions that exceed the measurement.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: A student says dye spreading proves that water molecules and dye particles have identical masses. Critique this inference.
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: Equal visual distribution implies equal particle masses
core1b.repair: List which variables the experiment measures and which remain undetermined.
core1b.boundary: Would two different dyes necessarily have the same diffusion rate?
core1b.model_response: Nothing in the observed final colour establishes equal particle masses. Diffusion is compatible with unequal molecular masses; independent measurements would be needed to estimate them.

subtopics.source_notes: Foundation topic; detailed lower-grade source alignment not yet reconciled.

deep_dive.big_idea: The particle model is not just a slogan that matter contains tiny pieces. It explains several observations at once: dye disperses without stirring, a small amount of perfume can be detected away from its source and water can change phase while remaining water. The science begins by asking which observations support motion, spacing and conservation, and which microscopic details remain unmeasured.
reasoning_path: Specify the system: a closed beaker preserves its total matter even while solutes redistribute.
Keep a particle-count ledger. A uniform colour in a larger volume means spreading, not multiplication of dye molecules.
Distinguish observation from model: the visible colour gradient is recorded; random particle motion is the inferred cause.
Test an alternative explanation, such as stirring or chemical reaction, by controlling the conditions and checking whether chemical identity changes.

discovery.title: A dye diffusion storyboard
discovery.setup: Visualise three time-ordered snapshots of a sealed beaker containing the same number of coloured solute particles; positions change but particle identity does not.
discovery.predict: How can the observed colour become less concentrated near the starting point and more widespread without changing the number of solute particles?
discovery.observation: The conceptual model redistributes the same finite particle inventory throughout the accessible liquid volume.
discovery.interpretation: Spreading is explained by transport and random motion, not creation of matter.
discovery.limits: The picture does not measure diffusion coefficients, individual molecular trajectories or prove that convection is absent.

deep_dive.connection: Next we compare what particle separations and movement can explain about the different states of matter.

subtopics.title: States, particle motion and compressibility
subtopics.entry_question: Why is it difficult to squeeze liquid water into half its original volume but easy to compress air?
core1a_paragraphs: Solids tend to preserve shape as well as volume; liquids preserve volume approximately but flow; gases expand to fill the container. In a particle model, these behaviours arise from different typical separations, motion and intermolecular interactions.

Gas particles spend much of their time separated by significant empty space, so compressing a gas can reduce the average separation strongly. In liquids, particles are already close together; pressure has a far smaller effect on volume under ordinary conditions.

Temperature influences the distribution of particle kinetic energies. Warming normally increases the mean kinetic energy, but a familiar phrase such as 'higher temperature means particles move faster' needs care during phase changes, when added energy can change arrangement rather than temperature.
subtopics.representation: Three equal-size boxes depict closely packed ordered solid particles, disordered close-packed liquid particles and widely separated gas particles. A fourth box compresses a gas while keeping particle number fixed.

worked_example.problem: A sealed syringe contains air. The outlet is closed while the piston moves inward. Explain the change.
steps: Take the same gas sample before and after compression.
The number of gas particles remains fixed if the syringe is sealed.
The container volume decreases, reducing typical particle separation.
Collisions with the walls become more frequent under comparable temperature.
worked_example.result: Air volume decreases substantially, with increasing pressure if conditions otherwise permit.
worked_example.check: The gas particle count should not change in a leak-free model.

misconception.wrong: Gases compress because their molecules shrink.
misconception.why: Compression primarily changes separation between molecules, not their molecular dimensions.
misconception.repair: Draw the same-sized particles in a smaller box with reduced gaps.

demands.title: Compression and particle separation
demands.core1a_explanation: Connect particle spacing with bulk compressibility, while accounting for a sealed container and constant particle identities.
demands.worked_reasoning: Halve the syringe volume without losing air. Same particles, smaller typical distances; pressure generally rises.
demands.independent_check: Identify the system boundary and whether the particle number is fixed.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: A sealed air syringe compresses easily, but the same syringe filled with water barely compresses. Explain.
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: Compression removes atoms from the gas
core1b.repair: Keep the particle number fixed and vary separation in the model.
core1b.boundary: What would happen if the syringe valve were accidentally open?
core1b.model_response: Air particles are separated by much greater gaps than liquid water molecules. A decreasing container volume mainly closes gas gaps; the densely packed liquid resists compression.

demands.title: Select appropriate state model
demands.core1a_explanation: A model should distinguish mobility, fixed relative positions and compressibility rather than use 'particles far apart' for every state.
demands.worked_reasoning: The gas model predicts large volume response to pressure; the liquid model predicts flow but small ordinary compressibility.
demands.independent_check: State a second independent condition before identifying the state.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: A mystery sample takes container shape but keeps almost unchanged volume under modest pressure. Which state model fits and what additional check helps?
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: Anything taking container shape must be a gas
core1b.repair: Test compressibility and volume independence along with shape.
core1b.boundary: Could a flowing granular solid mimic some liquid observations?
core1b.model_response: Liquid is plausible: flows to container shape but resists compression. Check a free surface, volume response over several containers and temperature conditions.

demands.title: Beware a model outside its boundary
demands.core1a_explanation: Particle sketches are idealisations; extreme pressure or temperature can change state or invalidate a simple picture.
demands.worked_reasoning: A gas under strong compression may liquefy if temperature allows; then the ordinary gas-separation rule no longer applies.
demands.independent_check: Acknowledge model limits rather than promising universal compressibility.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: Evaluate 'Every gas can be compressed to arbitrarily small volume by squeezing harder at a fixed temperature.'
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: The sparse-gas drawing is exact at any pressure
core1b.repair: State the pressure/temperature limits and possible phase transitions.
core1b.boundary: Would the same argument apply above a substance's critical temperature?
core1b.model_response: False. Real molecules occupy space and exert interactions; at suitable conditions a gas may liquefy. The idealised sparse-gas model cannot be extrapolated indefinitely.

subtopics.source_notes: Foundation chemical-particle interpretation; not a mathematical gas-law requirement.

deep_dive.big_idea: The everyday labels solid, liquid and gas describe bulk behaviour, but the microscopic explanation is more precise: solid particles often have comparatively constrained relative positions, liquid particles can rearrange while staying close together, and gas particles move through far larger average separations. The simple picture has limits—glasses, foams, powders and supercritical fluids require care.
reasoning_path: Observe shape and volume independently. A liquid flows to fit its vessel while maintaining approximately the same volume.
Use particle separation to explain why ordinary gases are much easier to compress than liquids; compression does not require molecules to shrink.
Connect heating with particle kinetic energy only in a comparable single phase. At a phase transition, incoming energy can rearrange particles instead of raising temperature.
Check the system boundary when interpreting a change of pressure or volume; air escaping from an open syringe makes the sealed-gas model invalid.

discovery.title: The two syringes comparison
discovery.setup: Compare two conceptual sealed syringes with the same plunger geometry, one containing air and one containing water. This is a simulation/thought experiment, not a procedure to force pressurised syringes.
discovery.predict: Which plunger moves farther under the same modest applied pressure and why?
discovery.observation: The air volume changes much more than the water volume under ordinary conditions.
discovery.interpretation: Compressibility tracks available particle separation and interactions, not a reduction in molecular size.
discovery.limits: At extreme pressures gases become non-ideal and may liquefy; liquid compressibility is small, not mathematically zero.

deep_dive.connection: Particle motion in a single phase also explains the observable spreading studied in diffusion.

subtopics.title: Diffusion and mixing
subtopics.entry_question: Why does the smell of food move through a room even when no fan is running?
core1a_paragraphs: Diffusion is a net spread of particles from regions of higher concentration into less concentrated regions as a result of random motion. Individual particles move in many directions; the net redistribution follows a concentration gradient.

Temperature changes particle motion and can affect diffusion rates. However, the observed speed of a smell also depends on air movement, ventilation, obstacles and how the odorous substance evaporates from the food.
A demonstration should distinguish pure diffusion from convection: warm air rising can transport vapour rapidly. We should never diagnose a single mechanism when the experiment permits several.
subtopics.representation: Use random arrows to show molecules moving in all directions and shading for the concentration gradient. A separate large air-flow arrow represents bulk convection; do not confuse the two.

worked_example.problem: Perfume is sprayed at one end of a still room. Describe why it becomes detectable farther away.
steps: Volatile fragrance molecules enter the air.
Thermal motion gives them changing random trajectories.
Particles gradually spread into previously dilute regions.
Air currents may additionally transport the molecules.
worked_example.result: Diffusion contributes to spreading; room air movement can accelerate transport.
worked_example.check: No source term is required after spray ceases; the total in a closed room is conserved.

misconception.wrong: Each perfume molecule travels directly from the source toward the observer.
misconception.why: Random molecular movement produces net spreading without directed intentions.
misconception.repair: Distinguish random particle trajectories from the evolving concentration profile.

demands.title: Random motion with net gradient
demands.core1a_explanation: Random motion occurs in both directions, yet more particles leave a dense region than enter it because the count is higher there.
demands.worked_reasoning: Take two equal adjacent volumes with 100 and 5 fragrance particles. Random crossing from the dense region gives more net outward crossings until concentrations approach.
demands.independent_check: At equilibrium net flux approaches zero; motion persists.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: How can a net diffusion flux occur when no molecule 'knows' which way to move?
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: Diffusion requires particles to move only downhill
core1b.repair: Separate one-particle motion from net statistical movement.
core1b.boundary: At equal concentration, does particle movement stop?
core1b.model_response: Individual motion is random, but a higher concentration yields more particles available to cross a boundary in that direction. The statistical imbalance creates net transport toward lower concentration.

demands.title: Diffusion versus bulk airflow
demands.core1a_explanation: Observed transport can combine diffusion with convection. Select models based on controls, not just distance and time.
demands.worked_reasoning: Repeat a perfume test with controlled air currents to distinguish bulk transport from molecular diffusion.
demands.independent_check: Compare predictions with and without airflow.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: Odour reaches a sensor much faster with a running fan. What model or combination best explains the change?
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: Any spreading through gas is pure molecular diffusion
core1b.repair: Introduce a control condition for airflow.
core1b.boundary: Would a completely sealed still-air box produce exactly the same time trace?
core1b.model_response: Bulk airflow carries the odour and adds advection to diffusion. Running the fan changes air-motion conditions, so speed alone does not measure molecular diffusion.

demands.title: Evaluate experimental inference
demands.core1a_explanation: A single travel-time observation generally underdetermines both diffusion rate and convection speed.
demands.worked_reasoning: An odour front 3 m away appears after 5 s, but a hidden ventilation stream may be present. One measurement cannot yield a unique molecular diffusion coefficient.
demands.independent_check: Infer only parameters that the controlled experiment identifies.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: A lab report infers a molecular diffusion constant solely from the first moment a smell is detected across a room. Is that justified?
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: A subjective smell detection is a calibrated molecular concentration
core1b.repair: Specify missing controls and measured quantities.
core1b.boundary: How could an electronic calibrated concentration sensor improve the result?
core1b.model_response: No. Detection threshold, source evaporation, air convection and room geometry are uncontrolled. Independent concentration-versus-time measurements under controlled airflow are needed.

subtopics.source_notes: Foundational diffusion, with optional high-complexity experiment inference.

deep_dive.big_idea: Diffusion is a statistical effect. Every individual particle can wander in either direction, yet the region with higher particle concentration sends more particles across a boundary on average. This is why net transport can have a direction without any molecule possessing a goal or a steering mechanism.
reasoning_path: Draw two equal adjacent regions and count how many diffusing particles occupy each at the initial time.
Allow random jumps in both directions. The side with more particles usually yields more transfers simply because it contains more candidates to move.
Explain why the net transfer declines as concentrations become similar even though the random motion itself continues.
Distinguish diffusion from convection: a fan moves air as a bulk fluid and can greatly accelerate detectable transport.

discovery.title: Random-crossing thought experiment
discovery.setup: Start with ten coloured particles on the left and two on the right of a permeable conceptual boundary; assume every particle has the same chance to cross in a short interval.
discovery.predict: Which side is expected to send more particles across, and do particles on the dilute side ever travel toward the concentrated side?
discovery.observation: Both directions occur, but the larger left population usually produces more expected left-to-right crossings.
discovery.interpretation: The net gradient-driven transfer is a population imbalance in random motion, not a force compelling each individual molecule.
discovery.limits: This simple discrete model ignores flow, concentration-dependent interactions and specific chemical reactions.

deep_dive.connection: The same random motion underlies evaporation, but evaporation also introduces an energy-transfer condition.

subtopics.title: Interconversion of states
subtopics.entry_question: When ice melts, what happens to the identity of its H₂O molecules?
core1a_paragraphs: Melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation, sublimation and deposition are physical changes of state. They alter particle arrangement, relative mobility and often intermolecular separation without requiring a new chemical species.

The direction of a phase change depends on temperature, pressure and energy transfer. Melting involves the solid becoming liquid, while vaporisation involves particles entering the gas phase. At a given pressure, a pure substance may have a characteristic transition temperature.

A phase-change diagram should track both phase and energy. If the sample is heated in an open container, its mass may decrease by evaporation even though no chemical decomposition occurs; apparent mass loss is not automatic evidence of reaction.
subtopics.representation: Sketch one water molecule H–O–H remaining intact in both a close-packed liquid arrangement and distant gas arrangement. Mark 'intermolecular attractions' separately from the intramolecular O–H bonds.

worked_example.problem: A sealed container holds ice that is allowed to melt completely. Is mass conserved and is the chemical formula changed?
steps: Define the system: closed container and the same water sample.
The solid arrangement changes to a mobile liquid arrangement.
Individual molecules remain H₂O.
Mass is conserved in the sealed system.
worked_example.result: Mass remains constant; the substance remains H₂O.
worked_example.check: Particle count and elemental identity are unchanged.

misconception.wrong: Melting breaks H₂O into hydrogen and oxygen.
misconception.why: Melting changes physical arrangement, not the covalent O–H connectivity.
misconception.repair: Keep molecule symbols intact when drawing the before/after stages.

demands.title: Physical state versus molecular identity
demands.core1a_explanation: Intermolecular arrangement can change while chemical identity stays fixed.
demands.worked_reasoning: Solid ice and water vapour still contain H₂O molecules. Their relative positions and motion differ.
demands.independent_check: Check elemental composition of a closed sample.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: Explain why boiling water does not normally produce hydrogen gas.
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: Temperature rise necessarily breaks covalent bonds in each water molecule
core1b.repair: Separate bonds within molecules from forces between molecules.
core1b.boundary: Is water vapour chemically distinguishable from liquid water by its formula?
core1b.model_response: Ordinary boiling separates intact H₂O molecules into the vapour phase; splitting O–H bonds would be a chemical reaction, not the phase change.

demands.title: Track matter across phase boundaries
demands.core1a_explanation: Conservation should be applied to the system you choose, not a visually selected vessel that may be open.
demands.worked_reasoning: An open pot loses water mass as vapour escapes; a sealed setup retains the same water across its phases.
demands.independent_check: The sum includes escaped and condensed vapour.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: A pan of boiling water loses 20 g of mass. Does this violate conservation of mass? Select a system model.
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: A lower vessel reading proves matter is destroyed
core1b.repair: Draw a system boundary and account for vapour beyond it.
core1b.boundary: What change would a sealed condenser make to measured total mass?
core1b.model_response: No. The weighed pan is open; 20 g water has escaped as vapour to the surroundings. A sufficiently inclusive closed system conserves mass.

demands.title: Evaluate a phase-change explanation
demands.core1a_explanation: A valid conclusion about physical change must state what has and has not been measured.
demands.worked_reasoning: A sealed flask changes appearance from ice to liquid while its mass remains constant. This supports phase change; if reactions were possible, extra identity evidence might be required.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: A student argues 'Mass conservation proves that no chemical reaction occurred.' Is this inference valid?
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: Only physical changes conserve mass
core1b.repair: Conservation applies to chemical reactions as well; propose a discriminating observation.
core1b.boundary: Would complete combustion in a closed vessel conserve total mass?
core1b.model_response: No. Chemical reactions in closed systems also conserve mass. Mass equality alone cannot distinguish physical from chemical changes; species identity or other evidence is needed.

subtopics.source_notes: Core physical changes with scientific inference emphasis.

deep_dive.big_idea: A melting ice cube seems to disappear, yet its chemical inventory need not change. We must keep two scales separate: the O–H bonds inside each water molecule and the collective organisation of many water molecules. Melting, freezing, evaporation and condensation affect the latter under ordinary conditions.
reasoning_path: Define the chemical species before and after the proposed process. For physical water phase changes both are H₂O.
Describe particle movement and average separation in ice, liquid water and water vapour without converting a molecule into its elemental gases.
Use a mass ledger for the declared system. A closed container retains its total water; an open vessel may lose vapour to the surroundings.
Test whether an observed bubble is a phase change rather than a chemical gas product by identifying the gas species where relevant.

discovery.title: A closed ice-to-water ledger
discovery.setup: Imagine a sealed transparent vessel that initially contains ice and a little empty headspace, then reaches a warmer equilibrium.
discovery.predict: Can the vessel's total mass change as the ice melts? Which microscopic arrangement changes?
discovery.observation: A sealed vessel keeps its total mass while the solid reorganises as liquid; the molecular formula H₂O is unchanged.
discovery.interpretation: The phase change affects the arrangement and energy of the molecules, not the identity of the elements.
discovery.limits: The detailed water phase diagram depends on pressure and hydrogen bonding; the school sketch is an approximation.

deep_dive.connection: Energy transfer during evaporation is a more demanding case because escaping molecules carry energy away.

subtopics.title: Evaporation and cooling
subtopics.entry_question: Why can evaporation cool the remaining liquid even on a warm day?
core1a_paragraphs: Liquid particles have a spread of kinetic energies, rather than all moving at exactly the same speed. Some particles near the surface have enough energy to escape into the gas phase at temperatures below the bulk boiling point.

Particles that escape carry away energy. If the remaining liquid is not supplied with enough energy from the surroundings, its average kinetic energy and temperature can fall. This is evaporative cooling.

Rate of evaporation depends on exposed surface area, temperature, air movement, relative humidity and the substance. Cooling can be reduced or reversed if external heating compensates for the energy removed. The explanation must include that energy balance.
subtopics.representation: Draw liquid molecules with a spread of motion-arrow lengths. Show some high-energy surface molecules escaping; the remaining ones have lower average energy unless heat enters.

worked_example.problem: Why does rubbing alcohol feel cool on the skin?
steps: Alcohol evaporates readily from the skin surface.
Molecules that leave remove energy from the liquid/skin interface.
Heat flows from the skin to support further evaporation.
The skin temperature can drop, giving a cooling sensation.
worked_example.result: Evaporation transfers energy away from the skin.
worked_example.check: Blocking evaporation should reduce the cooling effect under comparable conditions.

misconception.wrong: Evaporation only occurs at the boiling point.
misconception.why: Surface molecules can escape below the bulk boiling point.
misconception.repair: Distinguish surface evaporation from bulk boiling.

demands.title: Energetic mechanism of evaporation
demands.core1a_explanation: Connect a molecular energy distribution, surface escape and cooling of the remaining sample.
demands.worked_reasoning: Fast-escaping molecules remove more-than-average energy from the liquid and the environment may supply replacement heat.
demands.independent_check: Check an energy pathway, not just the sensation.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: Explain why wet clothes can feel cold in moving air even when the air is warm.
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: Moving air makes the liquid chemically colder without transferring energy
core1b.repair: Include an energy flow ledger and the role of humidity.
core1b.boundary: Would the same cooling occur if humidity were already near saturation?
core1b.model_response: Evaporation removes energy. Moving air carries away humid boundary-layer air and can speed evaporation; if energy supply is limited, the fabric and nearby surface cool.

demands.title: Which conditions control evaporation?
demands.core1a_explanation: A rate prediction requires surface area, airflow, temperature and humidity, not one-factor memorisation.
demands.worked_reasoning: A wide shallow dish often loses water faster than a narrow deep glass at similar temperatures because its exposed area is larger.
demands.independent_check: Explain both water-vapour gradient and energy.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: Two identical wet towels dry at different speeds in still humid air and moving dry air. Choose a causal model.
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: Evaporation depends only on water temperature
core1b.repair: List and control the main environmental variables.
core1b.boundary: Can evaporation slow in hot but very humid air?
core1b.model_response: The moving dry air more effectively removes water vapour near the towel and maintains a concentration gradient for evaporation. Heat transfer and temperature should also be considered.

demands.title: Reject an absolute cooling claim
demands.core1a_explanation: Evaporation removes latent energy but the measured temperature depends on net energy exchange.
demands.worked_reasoning: A surface undergoing evaporation in sunlight may warm if incoming radiation exceeds evaporative heat loss.
demands.independent_check: State the energy-balance condition needed for a temperature decrease.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: Evaluate: 'If a liquid evaporates, its temperature must always decrease.'
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: Evaporation is the only energy pathway
core1b.repair: Compare heat input and evaporative energy removal.
core1b.boundary: What would happen if a heater exactly compensates the evaporative loss?
core1b.model_response: False. Evaporation removes energy, but simultaneous heating may replace that energy or exceed the loss. Temperature depends on net energy balance.

subtopics.source_notes: Foundation; quantitative phase-energy models separately scope-reviewed.

deep_dive.big_idea: Evaporation cooling is an energy-flow story, not magic coldness created by the wind. At a liquid surface, some molecules escape into the surrounding gas; their escape requires energy. If the surrounding surface does not replace the lost energy fast enough, the liquid and what it touches cool.
reasoning_path: Recognise that molecules within a liquid have a distribution of kinetic energies, even at one measured temperature.
Connect escape from a surface to removal of energy from the remaining liquid and surrounding interface.
List the environmental variables controlling escape: temperature, relative humidity, surface area and airflow near the surface.
Compare the energy leaving through evaporation with heat arriving through sunlight or a heater before predicting the measured temperature change.

discovery.title: Two drying conditions
discovery.setup: Consider two identical damp cloths with equal starting temperature and exposed area. One is in humid still air and the other in moving dry air; no real experiment is required.
discovery.predict: Which is likely to dry faster and what energy exchange produces a temporary cooling sensation?
discovery.observation: Moving dry air typically removes the vapour-rich boundary layer and permits faster evaporation, carrying away energy.
discovery.interpretation: The rate and cooling depend on both the vapour concentration gradient and net heat transfer.
discovery.limits: Airflow can also warm the cloth; temperature need not decrease if incoming heat exceeds evaporative loss.

deep_dive.connection: A heating curve is another example in which energy transfer and temperature change are not interchangeable.

subtopics.title: Heating curves and latent heat (scope check)
subtopics.entry_question: Why can an ice-water mixture continue absorbing heat while the thermometer stays near the melting temperature?
core1a_paragraphs: At a pure substance's phase transition under approximately constant pressure, some added energy changes the microscopic arrangement rather than increasing the temperature. Temperature reflects a thermal state, but it is not a direct measure of every contribution to internal energy.

During ice melting near normal atmospheric pressure, energy is needed to disrupt parts of the organised solid structure. A simple heating curve therefore has sloping segments during single-phase warming and a roughly horizontal segment while melting proceeds.

The energy needed to melt a mass m of a substance at its transition temperature can be expressed as Q = mL, where L is the specific latent heat of fusion. This is scope-review material here: the proportionality is introduced for sense-making, not asserted as compulsory NSEJS mathematics.
A plateau depends on assumptions such as a reasonably pure substance, controlled pressure and sufficient mixing. Impurities and changing conditions can broaden a transition range.
subtopics.representation: Sketch a temperature-versus-energy plot: sloping solid heating, flat melting, sloping liquid heating. Label the plateau as energy used for phase change, not 'heater turned off'.

worked_example.problem: A 0.10 kg pure ice sample at 0°C absorbs 33.4 kJ at atmospheric pressure. Take Lf = 334 kJ/kg. What happens?
steps: Energy for completely melting the ice is Q = mLf.
Substitute 0.10 kg × 334 kJ/kg = 33.4 kJ.
The supplied energy matches the latent heat requirement for complete melting.
Under ideal assumptions, the final sample can be liquid water at about 0°C before extra warming energy is added.
worked_example.result: The ice just finishes melting, with little temperature rise during the transition.

misconception.wrong: A horizontal heating curve means no energy enters the material.
misconception.why: Energy can increase internal energy through the phase transition without an immediate temperature rise.
misconception.repair: Track heat input and microscopic changes separately.

demands.title: Energy during phase transition
demands.core1a_explanation: Energy conservation connects heater input to phase change while temperature is approximately fixed.
demands.worked_reasoning: For ice at its melting temperature, supplied heat changes solid to liquid rather than warming the liquid until melting is complete.
demands.independent_check: Point to the phase fraction and heat-input assumptions.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: Explain why a melting sample can remain near 0°C while energy continues entering.
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: No thermometer rise means no heat transfer
core1b.repair: Use energy bookkeeping and identify the changing phase fraction.
core1b.boundary: What does the heating curve do after all ice melts?
core1b.model_response: Near constant pressure, incoming energy supports the phase change rather than an increase in average thermal motion, so the temperature stays near the melting point until the ice is melted.

demands.title: Build a heating-curve ledger
demands.core1a_explanation: Different curve segments obey different energy relations. Identify phase state before applying a calculation.
demands.worked_reasoning: Heat absorbed while warming a single phase changes temperature, while a melt plateau uses Q=mLf under ideal assumptions.
demands.independent_check: Energy units and melt fraction ≤1 checked.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: A 0.20 kg ice sample at 0°C receives 33.4 kJ. Using Lf=334 kJ/kg, what fraction melts in an ideal setup?
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: 33.4 kJ must raise ice temperature by a fixed amount
core1b.repair: Check whether the sample is already at its transition temperature.
core1b.boundary: If 66.8 kJ entered, what phase would you expect?
core1b.model_response: Mass melted = 33.4 / 334 = 0.10 kg, so half the 0.20 kg melts. Remaining ice and water coexist near 0°C under stated conditions.

demands.title: When does a plateau stop being flat?
demands.core1a_explanation: The ideal pure-substance plateau assumes stable pressure and composition; changing these can alter the observed curve.
demands.worked_reasoning: Salt mixed into water can change the freezing/melting behaviour and broaden the transition range.
demands.independent_check: Distinguish instrument fault from physical alternatives.
hints: Identify the measured condition and the particles in the system.
Recall the relevant particle-model relationship without choosing the answer.
Check whether the same reasoning holds in a changed state or temperature.

core1b.predict: Before attempting the problem, predict the direction of the effect and identify the model you need.
core1b.attempt: A mixture shows a sloping 'melting' segment. Does that prove the thermometer is broken?
core1b.reconstruct: Work back from the particle-scale mechanism to the macroscopic observation, stating the conditions.
core1b.diagnose: Test the plausible wrong idea: All substances melt at one exact temperature regardless of composition
core1b.repair: Check purity and pressure before judging the curve.
core1b.boundary: What would you predict for a carefully purified sample at controlled pressure?
core1b.model_response: No. Mixtures may melt over ranges, and changing pressure, temperature gradients or impurities may prevent a simple pure-substance plateau. Instrument error is one alternative, not the only one.

subtopics.source_notes: Scope check: specific latent heat formula and quantitative curves may be extension depending on exact NSEJS source alignment.

deep_dive.big_idea: A pure substance heated through its melting transition does not necessarily rise steadily in temperature. On an ideal heating curve, a horizontal segment signifies that energy is being absorbed while solid changes to liquid. The system's total internal energy changes even though the thermal reading can remain near the melting temperature.
reasoning_path: Read the axes before interpreting a graph: time is not heat input unless power is known and approximately constant.
Identify single-phase sloping regions separately from a coexistence plateau where melting or boiling occurs.
For a pure sample at fixed pressure, use Q=mL only when the material is already at the relevant phase-change temperature.
Check purity, pressure and heat losses before expecting a perfectly horizontal experimental plateau.

discovery.title: A heating-curve identity check
discovery.setup: A simulated pure ice sample is held at 0°C while energy is supplied continuously; after all ice melts, heating continues.
discovery.predict: What happens to temperature while ice and water coexist, and after the last solid disappears?
discovery.observation: Under the ideal model the temperature remains near the melting temperature during coexistence and rises once liquid warming begins.
discovery.interpretation: A temperature plateau represents latent-energy absorption, not a disconnected heater.
discovery.limits: Specific latent heat arithmetic is scope-review material here; impurities and pressure changes can broaden or shift the transition.

deep_dive.connection: C02 will use these phase differences as property contrasts for separating mixtures.

chapter_spine.central_question: What can observations of ordinary matter tell us about invisible particles, motion and energy?
prior_knowledge: Everyday observations of air, water and solids
Reading a temperature scale and comparing measured quantities
Conserving matter in an identified closed system
journey: Infer particles from diffusion and mixing
Distinguish random diffusion from bulk flow
Track the same molecules across phase changes
Use energy balance to explain cooling and thermal plateaus
chapter_spine.chapter_closure: A physical explanation is strongest when it identifies particles, specifies conditions, predicts an observation and checks conservation. A phase change ordinarily rearranges molecules instead of changing their chemical identities.

key_terms.particle: A chemically specified atom, molecule or ion in a microscopic description.
key_terms.diffusion: Net spreading resulting from random molecular motion and concentration differences.
key_terms.phase: A physically distinct state or region of matter under stated conditions.
key_terms.evaporation: Escape of particles from a liquid surface into the gas phase.
key_terms.latent_heat: Energy per unit mass for a phase transition at a stated temperature and pressure, under appropriate assumptions.
